newsitem.title: USA: U.S. envoy Ross to travel to Mideast next week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy Ross to travel to Mideast next week.

text.p: U.S. special Middle East envoy Dennis Ross will travel to the region next week to try to help get the peace process back on track, the State Department said on Thursday.

"The president and Secretary (of State Madeleine) Albright are sending Ambassador Ross back again to consult further with the parties on the steps they're prepared to take to re-energise the process," department spokesman John Dinger told reporters.
After Ross returns to Washington, Dinger said, President Bill Clinton "will be making some judgments about how the United States can best help the parties make progress."
The trip will be Ross's second to the Middle East in two months. After his April trip, the United States said major gaps remained between Israel and the Palestinian Authority.
Dinger said he had no details of Ross's itinerary.

Albright, who drew criticism last week from a Palestinian official who said she needed to be more involved in Israeli-Palestinian negotiations, acknowledged she has not travelled to the region recently, but added, "the region has come to Washington."

"We have had more of the Middle East leaders in Washington since January than in a long time," Albright said. "...In addition to that, I have been on the phone with (Palestinian Authority) Chairman (Yasser) Arafat and with the Israelis and other parties involved in this."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Jordan's King Hussein both visited Washington in April, and the two men met privately in Minnesota, where the king had gone for prostate surgery.

"I think a very important issue for all of us is the Middle East and the necessity of the U.S. being involved there," Albright told reporters travelling with her to Moscow on Wednesday. "We have made quite clear that the U.S. will continue to play the role of broker, but the parties themselves have to give us more to work with."
Peace negotiations between the two sides have been suspended since Israel broke ground on a new Jewish settlement in traditionally Arab East Jerusalem on March 18.
On Wednesday, Netanyahu, speaking on CNN International, urged Palestinians to enter into talks on the tough issues yet to be negotiated.

The knotty so-called "final-settlement" issues include the fate of Palestinian refugees, Jewish settlers in occupied lands, borders and the future of East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967 and annexed but claimed by both sides.
